arithmetic.difference: `remember` updates the memory only when the organism is NOT on the remembered cell; `memory` updates on every step.
arithmetic.prediction_A: uniform field, one-shot choice -> survivors spread over many cells
arithmetic.prediction_B: uniform field, real memory -> survivors on few cells (all equal, nothing to learn)
arithmetic.prediction_C: gradient, real memory -> survivors at the right edge
arithmetic.why_B_is_specific: In a uniform field every cell is equally good, so a memory that keeps updating has nothing to prefer and the organism should not wander the way the one-shot chooser does. A smaller spread for B than for A is the signature of the update rule, not of the field.

fires.evidence: C: max cell 38 of 39 — a real memory must find the maximum of the gradient

silent.evidence: A: 32 distinct cells — must match EXP-07's 32-cell spread for the one-shot chooser

specific.evidence: B: 25 distinct cells vs A's 32 — the update rule must change the spread, not the field (both are uniform)

verdict.reason: the update rule changes the outcome: in the same uniform field the one-shot chooser spreads over many cells and the updating memory does not, and on a gradient the updating memory finds the maximum

limitations: One seed. Reproducibility across seeds is not checked here.
`Policy::Memory` was added in this experiment; it is not yet covered by the Rust test suite.
A uniform field is degenerate: there is no best cell, so the difference between the two rules may not appear on fields with a unique maximum.
The conclusion is about the update rule, not about memory in general.
